output.brief: The jump in write-offs is mostly an internal handling problem, not Haverlow's fault. Since the night receiving team was cut from six to four in week 31, chilled pallets wait a median of about 3h50 on an unrefrigerated dock (15–17°C) before reaching a chamber, up from 44 minutes. Night write-off rates rose from 0.6% to 2.9% for every supplier, while day-shift rates stayed flat. Haverlow's trailer data shows product at 2.4–3.5°C when the doors opened. The 6.5–8°C readings were keyed in hours later, after the product had warmed on the dock. The chambers held temperature. So the chargeback and the volume move would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Do not drop the night probe either, because that would hide the problem. Next step: restore night receiving to six, or otherwise get pallets into chambers fast, and set a maximum dock-to-chamber time tracked weekly from the scan data. Separately, sample Corriebank's claims against delivery lots to see whether the self-certified credits are over-claimed. That part is unproven. I'm fairly confident in the main finding. The Corriebank share is the open question.
